summary: Describes using the RSA digital signature algorithm as an authentication algorithm in IPsec's Encapsulating Security Payload (RFC 4303) and Authentication Header (RFC 4302). A digital signature gives data origin authentication where a shared-secret method such as HMAC cannot. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: Signing a letter with a signature only you can make, so anyone can check it came from you. This applies that idea to secure internet packets.

questions: rsa signatures in ipsec esp and ah
why use rsa signatures in ipsec
what rsa key size does rfc 4359 require
subtitle: Digital signatures for IPsec packets, so group members can tell who really sent a packet.

tldr.problem: When IPsec protects group traffic, every member shares one HMAC key, so any member can forge packets from another. HMAC proves the group sent a packet, not which member.
tldr.mechanism: The sender signs a SHA-1 hash of the authenticated packet bytes with its RSA private key, and the signature becomes the ESP or AH Integrity Check Value. Receivers verify it with the sender's public key.
tldr.outcome: Group applications get true data origin authentication, at the cost of much heavier processing and a packet tag of roughly 62 to 256 bytes.

today: RFC 4359 is a Proposed Standard from January 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its own text says SHA-1 was scheduled to be phased out in 2010, so it asks that later use be preceded by a suitability analysis.

sections.title: Why HMAC Is Not Enough for Groups
sections.content:
IPsec's Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP, RFC 4303) and Authentication Header (AH, RFC 4302) can protect unicast traffic and group traffic such as IPv4 and IPv6 multicast.

Between two entities, an HMAC transform is enough to prove who sent a packet, because only those two hold the key. In a group, all members share the single HMAC key, so any key holder can form a valid HMAC. The group-level property holds, but data origin authentication is not achieved.

Some group applications need true data origin authentication, where one member cannot impersonate another. An asymmetric signature algorithm such as RSA provides it: the sender keeps a private key and hands out the public key. This memo defines RSA signatures as an ESP and AH authentication mechanism.
sections.eli5: If everyone in a group uses the same secret handshake, anyone can fake being someone else. A signature only one person can make fixes that.

sections.title: Algorithm and Mode
sections.content:
The memo uses the RSA public key algorithm, chosen because verification is relatively efficient, which helps groups whose receivers have limited processing power. Two signature encodings are supported. RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 MUST be supported. RSASSA-PSS is believed to be more secure but was not ubiquitous at the time, and SHOULD be used whenever available. SHA-1 MUST be the hash.

To sign, the sender computes a SHA-1 hash of the authenticated portion of the AH or ESP packet, signs it with the private key and encodes the result. The resulting value is the Integrity Check Value (ICV). To verify, the receiver recovers the hash from the ICV with the public key, checks the encoding, computes its own SHA-1 hash of the authenticated bytes and compares the two.

For ESP the ICV equals the RSA modulus size. If the modulus is not a multiple of 8 bits, between 1 and 7 zero bits are prepended. For AH the ICV is also modulus-sized, with explicit ICV padding when the modulus is not a multiple of 32 bits (IPv4) or 64 bits (IPv6).

Key distribution and replacement interval are group policy. Using an ephemeral key pair with the lifetime of the SA is RECOMMENDED, which limits private key exposure to the life of the data it signs and removes any need to revoke the key pair.
sections.eli5: The sender squishes the packet into a short fingerprint and stamps it with a private stamp. Anyone with the matching public stamp-checker can see the stamp is genuine and the fingerprint still matches.

sections.title: Choosing the Key Size
sections.content:
The modulus size must be chosen carefully. Too small, and an attacker may rebuild the private key before the sender stops using it, which breaks data origin authentication. Too large, and the sender and every receiver waste CPU cycles. A conforming implementation MUST support a modulus size of 1024 bits.

The RFC cites key-size guidance and gives recommended maximum lifetimes for a key. It notes these are based on costs and analysis methods current when the guidance was published, so lifetimes should be revisited as those factors change.

sections.eli5: A lock that is too easy to pick is useless, and one that takes forever to open slows everybody down. You pick a lock that holds up just as long as you need it.

sections.title: Performance Costs
sections.content:
RSA is very costly in processing time compared with HMAC algorithms, though the cost is falling thanks to faster processors, faster software and hardware acceleration. Signature generation and key pair generation are much more expensive than verification, and those costs fall only on the sender.

RSA is best suited to traffic where the sender has substantial processing power and the traffic is small enough that an authentication tag of 62 to 256 bytes does not cause packet fragmentation. It should not be used when receivers are known to lack the power to verify signatures, and it should be used judiciously when any receiver may be battery powered.

A smaller modulus is acceptable if the protected traffic flows for less time than an attacker would need to find the private key. A low public exponent may lower verification cost.
sections.eli5: Signing is hard work for the signer, and checking is easier. It is great for a strong sender talking to many listeners, and a bad fit for tiny, weak devices.

sections.title: Interaction with ESP Ciphers
sections.content: RSA signatures cannot be used with an ESP Combined Mode algorithm that supplies its own explicit ICV. Such an algorithm adds the ESP ICV field itself, leaving no room for a separate authentication algorithm to do so. The RFC's example is the ESP Galois/Counter Mode algorithm (RFC 4106).
sections.eli5: If a toolkit already stamps its own seal on every package, you cannot add a second, different seal in the same spot.

sections.title: Key Management Requirements
sections.content:
Key management that negotiates RSA signatures MUST include the RSA modulus length, using the Authentication Key Length SA attribute. That lets a constrained device decline a key size it cannot verify. It MUST also include the encoding method, using the Signature Encoding Algorithm SA attribute.

A receiver needs the sender's public key. With a group key management system such as the Group Domain of Interpretation (RFC 3547), the public key SHOULD be sent as part of the key download policy, one per sender if there are several senders.

Using this transform for pairwise SAs, such as those negotiated by IKEv2 (RFC 4306), is NOT RECOMMENDED. An HMAC already gives data origin authentication there, so the value of the costlier signature is limited.
sections.eli5: Before anyone can check your signature they need a sample of it, and the group has to agree on how big and what kind of signature to use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The transform gives message modification integrity and host authentication, even when the message goes to a group. Non-repudiation is not claimed, since IP packets are ephemeral and not tied to any application.

Inserted or modified messages fail authentication and are dropped. Confidentiality, replay (handled by ESP and AH sequence numbers) and deletion are not addressed. A man in the middle cannot spoof the sender without the private key, provided the receiver got the public key in a trusted way.

A denial of service is possible: a packet that matches a valid SA and has a valid sequence number triggers an expensive signature check, and on multicast every member is hit at once. Wrapping the packet in an ESP or AH using an HMAC transform mitigates it, except against an attacker who holds the HMAC key.

The RFC says SHA-1 was scheduled to be phased out in 2010. Use of this transform after that date SHOULD be preceded by an analysis of its continued suitability.
sections.eli5: Fake or tampered packets get thrown away. But a bully could send lots of fake packets that look real enough to make receivers do slow checking work.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
The memo asks for new entries in the ISAKMP registry: an authentication algorithm with mnemonic SIG-RSA, an AH transform identifier with mnemonic AH_RSA, and two SA attributes. Authentication Key Length is a Variable type that carries the modulus size. Signature Encoding Algorithm is a Basic type that carries the encoding.

Encoding values: 0 Reserved, 1 RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5, 2 RSASSA-PSS. Values 3-61439 are reserved to IANA and need a Standards Action. Values 61440-65535 are for private use.
sections.eli5: The memo asks for official name tags and numbers for the new signature options so everyone uses the same ones.
